title: India Is Building an 'Unsinkable Aircraft Carrier' 150 Kilometres From the Malacca Strait.
excerpt: A ₹13,000 crore dual-use airport on Great Nicobar Island will give India a permanent military foothold at the mouth of the world’s busiest shipping lane.
body:
India has cleared a ₹13,000 crore ($1.4 billion) dual-use airport on Great Nicobar Island, its southernmost territory — a move that transforms a remote speck in the Andaman Sea into what defence planners are calling an "unsinkable aircraft carrier" at the mouth of one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.

The airport, to be built at Galathea Bay and completed within five years, will serve both Indian Navy operations and civilian aviation. It is the centrepiece of an ₹81,000 crore ($9 billion) megaproject that also includes an international container transhipment terminal with 14.2 million TEU capacity, a 450 MVA power plant, and a new township spread across 166 square kilometres.

## Why It Matters

Great Nicobar sits less than 150 kilometres from the western mouth of the **Strait of Malacca**, through which roughly one-third of global trade and the majority of East Asia's energy imports flow. By establishing a permanent military and logistics node here, New Delhi is positioning itself to monitor — and, if necessary, disrupt — the maritime corridor that China depends on for its oil, gas and manufactured exports.

The strategic rationale has sharpened dramatically since the Iran war broke out in February. With the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed and global energy supplies squeezed, control over alternate shipping chokepoints has become a first-order concern for every major Asian economy. India's bet is that a fortified Great Nicobar, equipped with a runway capable of handling strategic airlift and maritime patrol aircraft, gives it leverage that no aircraft carrier fleet can replicate.

"About 60 per cent of India's sea-based trade and a significant portion of its LNG imports pass through the Strait of Malacca," the Observer Research Foundation noted in a recent analysis. "The Andaman and Nicobar Islands are ideally placed to maintain stability in both the Bay of Bengal and the Andaman Sea."

## The China Factor

The project is explicitly designed as a counter to Beijing's growing Indian Ocean footprint. China has secured port access in Sri Lanka, Pakistan and Djibouti, and regularly deploys submarines and surveillance ships in waters India considers its strategic backyard.

Currently, around 75 per cent of India's transshipped cargo is handled by foreign ports — Colombo, Singapore and Port Klang. The transhipment terminal at Galathea Bay is designed to claw that traffic back, keeping both revenue and strategic visibility within national borders.

Defence analysts describe the initiative as a cornerstone of India's Act East policy and its MAHASAGAR doctrine — Mutual and Holistic Advancement for Security and Growth Across Regions — which frames New Delhi as a net security provider in the Indian Ocean.

## The Controversy

The project is not without opposition. Great Nicobar is home to the **Shompen**, a hunter-gatherer tribe with an estimated population of just 237, and the Nicobarese community of around 1,094 people. Environmental groups have raised concerns about the impact on the island's biosphere reserve, which hosts endemic species including the Nicobar scrubfowl and the giant leatherback sea turtle.

The government says the development follows a "sensitive and holistic approach" that considers indigenous communities and ecological resources. The project will use 130.75 square kilometres of forest land — a figure that has drawn criticism from conservationists who argue the scale is incompatible with meaningful environmental protection.

## What NRIs Should Watch

For the Indian diaspora, the Great Nicobar project signals a long-term strategic posture that will shape India's defence spending, trade infrastructure and geopolitical positioning for decades. The transhipment terminal alone could redirect billions in logistics revenue that currently flows to Singapore and Sri Lanka. And in a world where maritime chokepoints are increasingly contested — from Hormuz to Malacca — India's ability to project power from its island territories may matter more than any diplomatic communiqué.

The airport's decision to choose Galathea Bay over expanding the existing INS Baaz naval air station reflects a deliberate scaling of ambition: this is not a military outpost being upgraded, but a new strategic node being built from scratch.
